summary: Uzbekistan admits citizens of about 90 countries and territories — including the whole EU, the UK, the United States, Japan, South Korea, Canada, Australia and New Zealand — visa-free, most of them for 30 days. 44 other nationalities use the inexpensive USD 20 eVisa, and the rest apply at an Uzbek embassy.

currencyLimits.text: Cash worth USD 10,000 or more must be declared on entry on the written customs declaration — fill in two copies and make sure customs sign and stamp both. You cannot leave Uzbekistan with more foreign currency than you brought in, and undeclared currency may be confiscated.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Uzbekistan travel advice: entry requirements

notes: Drones may not be brought into Uzbekistan without prior government permission. They are confiscated at the border.
Some codeine-based and psychotropic medicines are controlled. Carry prescriptions and only personal quantities.

payments.text: Visa and Mastercard now work in hotels, restaurants and supermarkets across Tashkent, Samarkand and Bukhara, and city ATMs dispense both so'm and dollars, but bazaars, shared taxis and rural guesthouses remain cash-only.

safety.text: The UK government does not advise against travel to any part of Uzbekistan. Pickpocketing and bag-snatching are common in crowded places such as bazaars and on public transport, and terrorist attacks cannot be ruled out. You must carry your passport at all times — police often check.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Uzbekistan travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: Spring (April–May) and fall (September–October) are ideal for the Silk Road cities; July and August regularly top 40°C, and winters are cold but quiet.

idp.text: Uzbekistan is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Vienna, 1968), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Vienna, 8 November 1968 (UNTS vol. 1042, p. 17)

driving.text: Uzbekistan is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Uzbekistan yet.

tips.text: Every night in Uzbekistan must be registered. Hotels and licensed guesthouses do it automatically. Keep the small registration slips (or e-mails) until you leave, as border officers can ask for them; private hosts must register you through the Emehmon portal.
The Afrosiyob high-speed trains between Tashkent, Samarkand and Bukhara sell out days ahead in season. Book online or at the station as early as you can.
Do not bring a drone: import without prior permission is prohibited and devices are seized at the border, with fines possible.
Change money only at banks, exchange offices and ATMs. Rates are unified now, so the old black market offers no advantage and is illegal.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Uzbekistan?
faq.answer: Citizens of about 90 countries and territories, including the whole EU, the UK, Switzerland, the United States, Japan, South Korea, Israel, Türkiye, Malaysia, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, enter visa-free, most of them for up to 30 days. 44 other nationalities, among them India, Vietnam, Thailand, Egypt and much of South America, apply for the USD 20 eVisa at e-visa.gov.uz; nationalities the portal does not list apply at an Uzbek embassy.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Uzbekistan?
faq.answer: No. The official eVisa portal lists US citizens as visa-free for up to 30 days, for tourism or business. Longer stays or other purposes need a visa from an Uzbek embassy.

faq.question: How does the Uzbekistan eVisa work?
faq.answer: Apply at e-visa.gov.uz with a passport scan and photo. The single-entry eVisa costs USD 20, is normally issued within two working days, and allows a 30-day stay within a 90-day validity window; double-entry and multiple-entry versions cost USD 35 and USD 50.

faq.question: Do I have to register my stay in Uzbekistan?
faq.answer: Yes — accommodation must be registered for every night. Hotels and guesthouses do this automatically and give you slips or electronic confirmation; keep them until departure. Staying with friends or in an apartment requires registration through the official Emehmon system, and gaps can lead to fines on exit.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Uzbekistan visa-free?
faq.answer: The standard waiver allows 30 days per visit. Citizens of most CIS countries have more generous bilateral arrangements, and Kyrgyz citizens get 60 days. The eVisa also caps stays at 30 days — longer stays require an embassy visa or a fresh entry.
